toegepas.rede_vinder: The preposition meaning 'after' takes the accent, as the lesson itself writes 'Ná die ete' later.
toegepas.fout: The preposition 'after' is written without the accent here while the same lesson writes 'Ná die ete'.
toegepas.rede_keurder: A spelling fix that makes the lesson consistent with itself, with no change in meaning.

toegepas.rede_vinder: 'Na iemand vernoem' is the Afrikaans idiom for 'named after'; 'na iemand genoem' calques English.
toegepas.fout: 'Na iemand genoem word' is the looser form and can also be read as 'be called'.
toegepas.rede_keurder: 'Vernoem' is the exact Afrikaans verb for naming a child after someone, and the meaning stays the same.

toegepas.voor: Haar naam was Zanele en sy was
toegepas.na: Haar naam was Zanele, en sy was
toegepas.rede_vinder: AWS comma before 'en' joining two clauses that each have their own subject and verb.
toegepas.fout: There is no AWS comma before 'en' joining two clauses that each have their own subject and verb.
toegepas.rede_keurder: 'Haar naam was Zanele' and 'sy was oom Sipho se niggie' are two full clauses, so the AWS 2017 calls for the comma.

toegepas.voor: liefgehê word.” „In ons familie kies Ouma die eerste naam.
toegepas.na: liefgehê word. In ons familie kies Ouma die eerste naam.
toegepas.rede_vinder: Closing and reopening the quotation with no speaker between makes it read as a second speaker; it is all Zanele's speech, so it should be one quotation (protected wording left intact).
toegepas.fout: Closing and reopening the quotation with no speaker in between signals a new, unnamed speaker.
toegepas.rede_keurder: Only Zanele is speaking to Mila here, so one quotation fixes the stumble, and the protected wording stays intact word for word.

toegepas.na: die foto by tannie Elsa geneem
toegepas.rede_vinder: With Ouma Nomsa as subject, 'by haar' can be read as herself; naming tannie Elsa makes clear whose photo it was, as in the earlier 'die baba by tannie Elsa geneem'.
toegepas.fout: With Ouma Nomsa as the subject, 'by haar' leaves the reader to work out whose hands the photo came from.
toegepas.rede_keurder: Naming tannie Elsa makes the pronoun clear without adding anything, because she took out the photo in the sentences before.

toegepas.rede_vinder: 'Een ... op 'n slag' calques 'one at a time'; 'reël vir reël' is the natural Afrikaans.
toegepas.fout: 'Een reël op 'n slag' copies English 'one line at a time'.
toegepas.rede_keurder: 'Reël vir reël' is the natural Afrikaans, it is shorter and plainer for a Grade 6 reader, and it means the same thing.

laat_vaar.rede_vinder: A future seen from the past takes 'sou' in a past-tense narrative, matching 'die naam sou kies' in the previous sentence.
laat_vaar.rede_keurder: 'Gaan stry' with 'vandag' reads naturally as Mila's own fear in the story, and 'sou stry' adds a conditional colour while making the narrator's voice stiffer.

laat_vaar.rede_vinder: Lifting and holding a baby up is 'hoog ophou'; 'hoog hou' is unidiomatic here.
laat_vaar.rede_keurder: 'Die baba hoog gehou' is natural Afrikaans, and 'opgehou' could make a Grade 6 reader stumble on 'ophou' meaning 'stop'.

laat_vaar.rede_vinder: 'Bekommerd voel' echoes English 'felt worried'; 'was bekommerd' is the natural Afrikaans.
laat_vaar.rede_keurder: 'Bekommerd gevoel' is ordinary, natural Afrikaans rather than an anglicism, so swapping it is a lateral move in the author's voice.

laat_vaar.na: Mila het dit nog altyd geweet
laat_vaar.rede_vinder: 'Nog altyd' is the Afrikaans for 'had always known' up to that moment; bare 'altyd' reads as habitual.
laat_vaar.rede_keurder: 'Mila het dit altyd geweet' already reads well against 'Vandag' that follows, so 'nog altyd' is only a different way of saying it in the story.

vlae.teks: Mila was twaalf jaar oud en vir die eerste keer in haar lewe 'n niggie.
vlae.rede: Grammatical but easy to misread: 'niggie' means both niece and cousin, and saying Mila 'was' a niggie for the first time is unusual. 'Het vir die eerste keer 'n niggie gekry' would read more naturally, but it changes the meaning slightly (a first female cousin, not her first cousin at all), so a writer should decide which is meant.
